node.label: William Cronon
node.date_label: Changes in the Land 1983 · Nature’s Metropolis 1991 · “The Trouble with Wilderness” 1995 · coverage through 2000
node.description: A historian of North American environments who treats ecological change as a two-way relation between people and the rest of nature, worked out through property, markets and ideas of nature. Changes in the Land (1983) assumes that 'the interactions of the two are dialectical' and finds in colonial New England not a choice between landscapes with and without people but 'two human ways of living, two ways of belonging to an ecosystem'. Nature’s Metropolis (1991) follows grain, lumber and meat between Chicago and its hinterland on the premise that 'city and country have a common history, so their stories are best told together'. 'A Place for Stories' (1992) asks environmental historians for 'stories about stories about nature', and 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995) calls wilderness 'quite profoundly a human creation'. Reviewers found the Chicago book distant from farmers and townspeople, or moralising; he replied that he saw 'no pure heroes or pure villains'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: William Cronon (b. 1954); Changes in the Land: Indians, Colonists, and the Ecology of New England (1983); “Modes of Prophecy and Production: Placing Nature in History” (JAH 1990); Nature’s Metropolis: Chicago and the Great West (1991); “Kennecott Journey: The Paths out of Town” (1992); “A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative” (JAH 1992); “The Uses of Environmental History” (1993); “The Trouble with Wilderness” (1995). Readings: the Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis, with his response (1992); Sessions’s reply on wilderness (1996); his own afterword to Changes in the Land (2003).
node.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-13: chapter 1 of Changes in the Land in an unpaginated web transcription; 'A Place for Stories' (JAH 1992; pp. 1347–1351 and 1369–1376 read) and 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993; OCR of the author’s scan, journal pagination); 'Kennecott Journey' (1992); passages of 'The Trouble with Wilderness' in the author’s reflow; and the 1992 Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis, with his response read in full. Nature’s Metropolis itself is unread: its words appear here only as forum contributors quote them with page numbers. 'Modes of Prophecy and Production', his 1990 response to Worster in the JAH round table, is paywalled and unread. He is not presented as a founder. He places environmental history among the 'new' histories 'born or reenergized in the wake of the 1960s' (1993, p. 2), names Nash, Hays, Worster, Merchant, Tarr and Pyne as practitioners (pp. 2–3), footnotes lessons to Crosby, Richard White, McEvoy and others (pp. 8–10), and echoes Leopold (n. 11). On Mahoney’s reading (1992, p. 492), Nature’s Metropolis demonstrates 'this fundamental urban historical premise' rather than inventing it. His approaches were contested in period: Danbom (1992, p. 503) finds 'environmental moralism'; Mahoney (p. 491) that urban and economic history 'seem only to serve the interests of environmental history'; Sessions (1996) that the wilderness essay underweights wild habitat. His 2003 afterword, McNeill (2003) and Canadian uses after 2000 are later readings.

proposed_edges.relationship: Ecological change as a two-way relation of people and nature, traced through property, markets and ideas of nature (1983–1995)
proposed_edges.map_label: Ecology, markets and ideas of nature, 1983–95
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cronon’s own in-period statements. Changes in the Land (1983), ch. 1 'The View from Walden', read in full in an unpaginated web transcription (page numbers not verified): 'The replacement of Indians by predominantly European populations in New England was as much an ecological as a cultural revolution'; 'An ecological history begins by assuming a dynamic and changing relationship between environment and culture, one as apt to produce contradictions as continuities. Moreover, it assumes that the interactions of the two are dialectical'; 'The choice is not between two landscapes, one with and one without a human influence; it is between two human ways of living, two ways of belonging to an ecosystem'; 'The pig was not merely a pig but a creature bound among other things to the fence, the dandelion, and a very special definition of property'; a 'world capitalist system' draws people 'into trade and market relations which lie well beyond the boundaries of their local ecosystems'. He sets this against species-transfer accounts 'as Alfred Crosby and William H. McNeill have done', which are 'bound to be incomplete', and against functionalist ecological anthropology, which risks 'a static and ahistorical view'. In 1992 he calls Nature’s Metropolis 'a natural sequel' to that book, which 'described a comparable set of environmental changes that occurred in New England as that region became linked to London’s markets' (Annals of Iowa forum, p. 517). 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993): the lesson 'When people buy and sell things in a market, they link together ecosystems and encourage change' is 'a central concern of my own work' (p. 8, n. 14, citing Changes in the Land, Nature’s Metropolis and 'Kennecott Journey'); 'The chief moral of my own version of environmental history is the one I tried to embed in the title of my book Changes in the Land. To live as human beings on this planet is to change the world around us' (p. 19); 'the material history of environmental change is simultaneously a spiritual history of human consciousness and a political economic history of human society' (p. 19); 'All environmental knowledge is culturally constructed and historically contingent—including our own' (p. 14), held together with the claim that 'the natural world exists quite apart from what we believe about it' (p. 15). 'Kennecott Journey' (1992, p. 33): 'The special task of environmental historians is to tell stories that carry us back and forth across the boundary between people and nature to reveal just how culturally constructed that boundary is—and how dependent upon natural systems it remains.' 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995, author’s reflow p. 1): wilderness is 'quite profoundly a human creation'. A contribution, not a founding: he makes the claim for materialist analysis that tries 'to finesse a full-blown determinism' on behalf of the field ('One important contribution of environmental history', 1993, p. 13), and places the field among the 'new' histories of the 1960s (p. 2). Contested in period: Danbom (1992) reads Nature’s Metropolis for its 'environmental moralism' (p. 503) and as 'a book about evil unleavened by good' (p. 506); Cronon answers 'I see no pure heroes or pure villains in the stories I tell' (p. 522). His 1990 JAH response to Worster is unread. The 2003 afterword (pp. 182–185: property analysis learned from anthropology, economics and legal theory; his own criticism of schematic capitalism and source asymmetry) is a later reading. edge_342 (anthropology → environment) and edge_343 (environment → culture) stay: they record anthropology as a resource and environmental history’s contribution to cultural history; this arrow is his own framework.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: colonial_property ('Property concepts help Cronon explain changes in New England'; works: Changes in the Land, with the 2003 afterword) holds him alone and is the book he names as the 'chief moral' of his environmental history (1993, p. 19). The edge’s claim is broader than the strand: urban_hinterland is carried in substance by edge 2, and wilderness_culture by edge_343 and the strands wilderness_contexts and wilderness_conservation_response. A reviewer who prefers a framework-level strand could add one (for example, 'Nature and culture in dialogue') at release.

proposed_edges.relationship: City and hinterland as one history of markets and environmental change: Chicago and the Great West (1991)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis (51, Summer 1992, pp. 480–525; Cronon’s response pp. 515–525 read in full, the commentaries in part). Cronon: 'One of my most important agendas in Nature’s Metropolis was to try to convince environmental historians that the city is among the most important historical loci of environmental change, and that they must therefore grapple with urban history if they wish to understand their own subject. Surely such an argument can only strengthen the claims of urban history as a field' (p. 520); 'one really can’t understand the history of nineteenth-century Iowa … if one fails to see those places, at least in part, as portions of Chicago’s hinterland' (p. 515). The editor, Marvin Bergman, quotes the book’s premise: 'city and country have a common history, so their stories are best told together' (p. 481, quoting p. xiv). Rohrbough quotes its frontier as 'a story of metropolitan expansion, of the growing incursions of a market economy into ever more distant landscapes and communities' (p. 488, quoting p. 378). The urban historian Timothy Mahoney judges that the book 'makes significant theoretical and substantive contributions to both economic and urban history by placing urban and economic development in an environmental context' and has, 'perhaps inadvertently, brought urbanization as a “process” forward' (p. 491). A contribution, not a founding: Mahoney calls the city–hinterland link 'this fundamental urban historical premise', whose explanatory power 'Cronon’s study of Chicago demonstrates' (p. 492). Contested in period: Mahoney writes that in the book 'urban and economic history seem only to serve the interests of environmental history' (p. 491). Cronon concedes the 'rather distant and abstract quality of a bird’s-eye view' (p. 518) and calls studies of hinterland responses 'a valuable corrective to the metrocentric story of Nature’s Metropolis' (p. 519). 'Kennecott Journey' (1992, p. 39) states the same mechanism at another site: consumption 'came to be increasingly separated from the place of ecological production'. The book itself is unread here. cronon_urban_reception (2022) is a later reading. edge_720 is the group-level arrow between the two entries; see the proposed relabel.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: city_hinterland ('Cronon follows commodities between rural production and urban processing and exchange'; work: Nature’s Metropolis) holds him alone and matches the checked argument. The other urbanhistory strands belong to other historians.

proposed_edges.relationship: Narrative bounded by evidence, ecology and the community of scholars: an environmental historian’s answer to postmodern critiques of narrative (1992)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 'A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative', JAH 78:4 (March 1992), author-hosted copy in journal pagination (pp. 1347–1351 and 1369–1376 read). Writing about narrative, 'we cannot avoid encountering the postmodernist assault on narrative, which calls into question not just the stories we tell but the deeper purpose that motivated us in the first place' (p. 1349). The argument is meant for all historians: 'I am urging historians to acknowledge storytelling as the necessary core even of longue durée histories … Environmental history is but one example of these, and most of my arguments apply just as readily to the others' (p. 1349, n. 5). 'I, like most practicing historians, am only willing to follow the postmodernists so far'; 'My goal throughout has been to acknowledge the immense power of narrative while still defending the past (and nature) as real things to which our storytelling must somehow conform lest it cease being history altogether' (p. 1372). Three bounds: 'our stories cannot contravene known facts about the past' and 'our stories must make ecological sense' (p. 1372); 'We write as members of communities' (p. 1373). 'To just that extent, nature coauthors our stories' (p. 1373). Against 'an endless postmodernist deconstruction of texts that fails to ground itself in history, in community, in politics, and finally in the moral problem of living on earth' he asserts 'the virtues of narrative' (p. 1374), and he asks environmental historians for 'not just stories about nature, but stories about stories about nature' (p. 1375). He reads with Hayden White’s Metahistory, Tropics of Discourse and The Content of the Form and with Novick (nn. 6, 7, 43), and credits Richard White with the argument about criticism (n. 46). The 1993 address restates it: historical wisdom 'usually comes in the form of parables, not policy recommendations or certainties' (p. 16). This is his own text; no in-period reading that places the essay in the postmodernism debate was read.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No truthdebate strand fits. practical_realism (Appleby, Hunt and Jacob: tentative knowledge, archival inquiry and democratic discussion) is closest in substance, since Cronon too grounds narrative in scholarly community, but the strand is about their 1994 book. disciplinary_scrutiny and evidence_representation are about Evans, Ginzburg and White. A reviewer could add a strand at release (for example, 'Narrative, nature and the limits of storytelling').
proposed_edges.include_note: Optional. Included because the essay addresses all historians (n. 5) and answers postmodern critiques of narrative explicitly, in the JAH, in the period of the truthdebate entry. The evidence is Cronon’s own text only: no in-period third-party reading of the essay was read. Drop the edge (include: false) if the bar is reception evidence, and keep 'A Place for Stories' in the node text.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: 'The Trouble with Wilderness' historicises wilderness as a cultural idea, but edge_343 (environment → culture) already records that contribution and disclaims influence on the whole cultural turn. No checked text shows cultural historians outside environmental history taking it up. A second arrow would repeat edge_343.

In 1992 he argues 'that economic history and environmental history have extensive areas of overlap, and that neither can be properly understood if one ignores the other' (Annals of Iowa forum, p. 520), and Mahoney credits contributions to economic history (p. 491). edge_267 (economic — environment comparison: Cronon, Worster, Pomeranz) already carries this; the reviews in economic journals (Runge, Land Economics 1993) were not read. Not proposed.

The forum editor chose Mahoney to represent 'economic historians and historical geographers as well as urban historians' (Bergman, p. 482), and Cronon assigned Sauer in 1994 (sauer_teaching_reception). No checked contribution to historical geography as a field; Harris’s review (Geographical Review 82:4, 1992) was not read.

Changes in the Land contrasts Indian and colonial land use, and the country_voice_comparison strand already uses it. His own 2003 afterword criticises the book’s uneven treatment of Indigenous sources; that is a later reading. No in-period text read here makes him a contributor to Indigenous history.

The only evidence is later and secondhand: a 2017 NiCHE blog report of an oral remark that Nature’s Metropolis incorporated Innis’s staples and metropolitan-hinterland theses, and a 2024 NiCHE post (canon-evidence-canada.md, R7 and R8). The recommendation’s separate Innis → environment edge is the place for this question.

'A Place for Stories' lists Hayden White’s Metahistory, Tropics of Discourse and The Content of the Form among many works on narrative (nn. 6–7). A reading list is not a genealogy; the use is recorded in the evidence of edge 3.

proposed.relationship: Environmental perspectives on city–hinterland connections, assessed in period by an urban historian as a contribution to urban history (1991–92)
proposed.evidence_note: In-period evidence: the 1992 Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis (open PDF, text layer read). The urban historian Timothy Mahoney judges that the book 'makes significant theoretical and substantive contributions to both economic and urban history by placing urban and economic development in an environmental context', and that Cronon 'has, perhaps inadvertently, brought urbanization as a “process” forward from its current relegation as a kind of assumed stage set for monographs on local occurrences in cities' (p. 491). Of the premise that 'to really understand how and why cities developed, one must study how they organized their hinterlands', he writes: 'Cronon’s study of Chicago demonstrates the explanatory power of this fundamental urban historical premise' (p. 492). He also finds that in the book 'urban and economic history seem only to serve the interests of environmental history' (p. 491). Cronon’s response: 'One of my most important agendas in Nature’s Metropolis was to try to convince environmental historians that the city is among the most important historical loci of environmental change'; 'Surely such an argument can only strengthen the claims of urban history as a field, setting the process of urbanization in a broader context that is as important to urban historians as it is to environmental ones' (p. 520). The arrow rests on one book, one urban historian’s in-period assessment and the author’s reply; it does not claim that urban history as a field adopted environmental questions. Context only, not support for the claim: Cronon’s 1993 ASEH address names Joel Tarr’s 'many studies of pollution and waste streams' (p. 3, n. 6) and cites Melosi’s Garbage in the Cities (n. 24). cronon_urban_reception (2022) is a later reading. Cronon’s own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (revision 1.131).

edge_720.alternative: Leave edge_720 unchanged if reviewers read it as environmental history’s contribution, with Cronon as its example.

verification.note: Open PDF (47 pp.) read in its text layer; Crossref 10.17077/0003-4827.9665 gives Annals of Iowa 51:5, July 1992, pp. 480–525. Read: editor’s introduction pp. 480–483 (Bergman, named in Cronon’s response); Rohrbough pp. 483–488; Mahoney pp. 490–493; Danbom pp. 500 and 503–506; Scarpino’s opening p. 506; Cronon’s response pp. 515–525 in full. Contributors quote the book with page numbers, including 'city and country have a common history, so their stories are best told together' (xiv, quoted p. 481), first and second nature (xvii, quoted p. 484) and the frontier as 'a story of metropolitan expansion' (378, quoted p. 488). Mahoney: contributions to economic and urban history 'by placing urban and economic development in an environmental context'; 'urban and economic history seem only to serve the interests of environmental history' (p. 491); the city–hinterland link as 'this fundamental urban historical premise' (p. 492). Danbom: 'environmental moralism' (p. 503); 'a book about evil unleavened by good' (p. 506). Cronon: the city 'among the most important historical loci of environmental change' (p. 520); Nature’s Metropolis as 'a natural sequel' to Changes in the Land (p. 517); the bird’s-eye view and 'the metrocentric story' conceded (pp. 518–519); 'no pure heroes or pure villains' (p. 522); the transition to capitalism as 'a complex, multistaged process' (pp. 523–524). The rest of Mahoney’s and Danbom’s essays and Scarpino’s pp. 507–515 were skimmed, not read closely. Cronon cites Coclanis’s hostile review (Reviews in American History 20, 1992, 14–20), which was not read.

cronon_wilderness.note: Author-hosted reflow PDF (24 pp., reflow page numbers in its running heads) re-read for the 1.131 person entry: wilderness 'is quite profoundly a human creation—indeed, the creation of very particular human cultures at very particular moments in human history' (reflow p. 1); 'wilderness represents a flight from history', and 'The removal of Indians to create an “uninhabited wilderness”' shows 'just how invented, just how constructed, the American wilderness really is' (p. 10); 'the trouble with wilderness is that it quietly expresses and reproduces the very values its devotees seek to reject' and its reproduction of 'the dualism that sets humanity and nature at opposite poles' (p. 11); the wilderness dualism 'denies us a middle ground in which responsible use and non-use might attain some kind of balanced, sustainable relationship' (p. 16); 'The autonomy of nonhuman nature seems to me an indispensable corrective to human arrogance' (p. 17); the tree in the garden and the tree in the wilderness (pp. 18–19). The reflow page numbers are not those of Uncommon Ground (69–90).
